title: Al-Ghazali's Revival
hook: forty books on worship, habits, what destroys and what saves

segments.voice: Yesterday, akhlaq, character, and your line: sent for character. Did you do your small act on purpose? Today, a book built to train it. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

A celebrated professor stands up to lecture in Baghdad, and nothing comes out. His tongue won't move. That's how Abu Hamid al-Ghazali tells it, in his own account of his life, called Deliverance from Error. He held a celebrated teaching post, and he had come to doubt that his learning was doing his soul any good. So he left the post, the students, the reputation, and went traveling. Out of that turn came a huge book with a bold title. Today, al-Ghazali's Revival.
screen: `A LECTURE THAT WON'T COME.` → `HE LEAVES IT ALL.` → `A BOOK WITH A BOLD TITLE.`

segments.voice: The book is Ihya Ulum al-Din, the Revival of the Religious Sciences. Look at the title. Revival means bringing back to life. Al-Ghazali's claim was that religious knowledge had grown dry: people knew the rules, argued the fine points, and the heart was left out. So he set out to put the heart back in. He tells us his plan in the introduction. The book has four quarters, with ten books in each. The first quarter is worship, with books among them on knowledge, belief, purity, prayer, charity, fasting, pilgrimage, the Qur'an, remembrance. The second is everyday life, the habits: eating, marriage, earning a living, friendship, travel. Then the turn inward. The third quarter is what destroys: the heart's diseases, like anger, envy, greed, showing off, pride. And the fourth is what saves: the heart's cures, like repentance, patience, gratitude, hope, love. Notice the order. You don't get to the soul's inner rooms by skipping the kitchen and the marketplace. The ordinary life comes first, and then the doctor examines the heart, sickness before cure. That's why this block on character keeps coming back to him. His book reads like a doctor's manual. Here is a vice, here is how it grows, here is how it's treated. And the cures he names become the stations we'll walk through in the coming days. What does that change? The Revival treats a bad temper the way you'd treat a sprained ankle: seriously, step by step, without shame, and with the expectation that it can heal.
screen: `REVIVAL: BRINGING THE HEART BACK.` · `WORSHIP, THEN EVERYDAY HABITS.` · `WHAT DESTROYS, THEN WHAT SAVES.` · then, large: `A DOCTOR'S MANUAL FOR THE HEART.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one chapter title. Here are a few from the Revival. The Book of Knowledge. The Book of the Etiquette of Eating. The Book of the Marvels of the Heart. The Book of the Dangers of the Tongue. The Book of Repentance. The Book of Patience and Gratitude. Settle, and breathe. Let one title choose you, the one that tugs a little. Hold it, and ask: what would a chapter about this say about my life? Don't write the chapter. Just open the question and sit with it. If you pray, you can ask Allah for beneficial knowledge. If not, let the title rest in you. The bell holds the time.
Al-Ghazali's Revival. The Ihya: a great work in four quarters, worship, habits, what destroys and what saves, written to bring the heart back into religious knowledge. Today's word.

Your line: the revival. Today, notice one ordinary habit, eating, speaking, working, and ask what it does to the heart. Tomorrow, the first station: repentance. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Students of the inward path read al-Ghazali's Ihya Ulum al-Din, the Revival of the Religious Sciences, sometimes book by book with a teacher.

myth: the Revival begins with the heart's diseases
it begins with worship, then everyday habits, and only then turns inward.
al-Ghazali describes leaving his teaching post after a crisis
in Deliverance from Error he tells of being unable to lecture, and leaving.
the Revival treats vices as things that can be treated, like an illness
it reads like a doctor's manual: the vice, how it grows, how it heals.

fork.setup: you're al-Ghazali, at the top of your field in Baghdad, and you doubt your learning is helping your soul. what do you do?
options: keep lecturing and push the doubt down.
leave the post and go traveling.
write a book refuting your doubts.
fork.reveal: in his own account, he left the post and the reputation, and the Revival grew out of that turn.
